title: First deadlock in a lock log
prompt:
Replay a log of threads acquiring and releasing locks, and return the index of the first event that leaves the threads deadlocked, or -1 if no event does.

- events[i] is [thread, action, lock]: thread and lock are strings, action is "acquire" or "release". Up to 10,000 events, 100 threads and 100 locks.
- acquire: if nobody holds the lock, the thread now holds it. Otherwise the thread becomes blocked and joins the back of that lock's waiting line.
- release: the thread gives up the lock. If the lock's waiting line is non-empty, the thread at its front leaves the line, is no longer blocked, and holds the lock immediately; otherwise the lock becomes free.
- Wait-for graph: each blocked thread points to the thread holding the lock it waits for. A deadlock exists when this graph has a cycle. Return the index of the first event after which there is a cycle.
- The log is consistent: a blocked thread has no events until it is unblocked, a thread never acquires a lock it already holds, and only releases locks it holds.
hints: Model the state as a graph: who holds each lock, and which lock is each blocked thread waiting for?
Each blocked thread waits for exactly one lock, which has exactly one holder, so every thread has at most one outgoing wait-for edge. Releases hand the lock to the front of a FIFO line per lock.

Only an acquire that blocks adds an edge, so any new cycle goes through that thread. Starting from the lock's holder, keep jumping to "holder of the lock this thread waits for"; hitting the new waiter means deadlock, hitting a non-blocked thread means no cycle.

solution.explanation: Track the holder of each lock, the lock each blocked thread waits for, and a FIFO line per lock for hand-offs. Only an acquire that blocks can add an edge, and every thread has at most one outgoing edge, so a new cycle must pass through the thread that just blocked. Follow holder -> waits-for -> holder from that lock; reaching the blocking thread means deadlock, reaching a running thread means none.

complexity.notes: m events, p threads, L locks. Each chain walk visits each thread at most once because the graph was acyclic before the event. The JS shift() on a waiting line is O(line length), which is at most p.

followUps: Acquiring locks in one global order (for example, alphabetical) makes deadlock impossible. Why?
Return the threads in the cycle as well, starting from the thread that blocked last.
